summary: Marks the 40th anniversary of the RFC document series with a short reflection. It is a commemorative memo rather than a technical specification.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo marks the 40th anniversary of the RFC series. It looks back at the series' beginnings and describes changes to the RFC Editor function over the previous ten years.

subtitle: The RFC Editor marks four decades of the RFC document series.

tldr.problem: The RFC series reached its 40th anniversary, prompting a reflection on its history and recent changes.
tldr.mechanism: The memo recalls RFC 1 and Jon Postel, then describes changes in RFC editing, funding, review and community input.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational commemorative memo. The unit metadata says RFC 8700 later updated it.

today: RFC 5540 is Informational and was updated by RFC 8700. The RFC is a commemorative account of the series at its 40th anniversary.

sections.title: RFC 1 and Jon Postel
sections.content:
The first Request for Comments, RFC 1, was published at UCLA on April 7, 1969. By the 40th anniversary, the series contained more than 5,400 documents and roughly 160,000 pages. It grew out of research that created the ARPANET and later the Internet.

After the IETF formed in the mid-1980s, RFCs became its primary publication vehicle for standards. Jon Postel served as RFC Editor for the first 29 years, with substantial help from Joyce K. Reynolds.
sections.plainLanguage: The first RFC appeared in 1969, and the series grew to thousands of documents. Jon Postel edited the series for its first 29 years, with help from Joyce K. Reynolds.

sections.title: Changes in the RFC Editor Function
sections.content:
After Postel died in October 1998, Joyce Reynolds and Bob Braden formed a small organization at USC/ISI to continue the RFC Editor function. Funding moved from the US government to the Internet Society. USC/ISI was selected to provide RFC Editor services from 2007 through 2009, and the memo expected a significant transition during 2009.

The RFC editorial process had become more efficient and transparent. The RFC Editor also formed an Editorial Board to help review RFCs in the Independent Submission stream, and created an email list for community input.
sections.plainLanguage: After Postel's death, colleagues continued the editorial work. Funding, review support and ways for the community to give input also changed.

sections.title: Security and Acknowledgment
sections.content: The memo says it raises no security issues. USC/ISI acknowledges that it had served the community for 31 years.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo reports no security issues. It closes by acknowledging USC/ISI's service to the community.

references.text: RFC Editor, et al., "30 Years of RFCs", RFC 2555, April 1999.
